summary:
Gauteng stands under the national constitutional framework of South Africa. The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation; the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) of 2000 gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court, which also hears hate-speech and harassment complaints; and the Prevention and Combating of Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act, signed in May 2024, explicitly names sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics as protected grounds. No consensual-conduct offence engages a visitor on the basis of gender identity or sexual orientation: sodomy and the common-law 'unnatural sexual offence' were struck down in 1998 with retroactive effect to 1994, and the residual disparity in the age of consent was equalised at a gender-neutral 16 by the 2007 statute, the old disparity being confirmed unconstitutional in Geldenhuys v NDPP in 2008.

Legal gender recognition has been available since the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003, which permits amendment of sex status in the population registry and the issue of identity documents and passports reflecting gender identity. The statute requires medical or surgical treatment, including hormone replacement therapy, but not sex reassignment surgery. Identity documents remain strictly binary, so non-binary people cannot be recognised, and the medical requirements lock some people out of recognition altogether. In October 2021 the Department of Home Affairs announced plans for gender-neutral identification on South African ID cards, an identity-management document estimating 530,000 non-binary residents, but officials confirmed the change would take a few years as it passes through consultation to legislation.

On 10 November 2025 the Gauteng Division of the High Court in Johannesburg, sitting as an Equality Court, delivered judgment in Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre and Others (Case No. 2024/070075). The court held that the Department of Correctional Services engaged in unfair discrimination and harassment of a transgender inmate by refusing to let her express her gender identity and by denying prescribed gender-affirming hormone therapy, and that the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment includes gender-affirming hormonal therapy at state expense. The orders require the Department to provide that treatment, to permit clothing and cosmetics expressing her gender identity, to implement the required accommodations, and to enforce its own standard operating procedures for transgender inmates. The South African Human Rights Commission's National Preventive Mechanism welcomed the ruling on 14 November 2025 as an affirmation of the rights of transgender persons in correctional facilities.

The judgment is also the only documented determination of where a trans prisoner is housed in Gauteng. Mokoena, a transgender woman serving a life sentence, was held at Johannesburg Correctional Centre: first in Medium A section, where she could express her gender identity through long hair, makeup and women's clothing, then transferred to Medium C section, and at the time of judgment housed in C Single Section, a segregated single-confinement unit. Despite requesting a single cell she was accommodated with cisgender male cellmates, first two cisgender gay men and then one cisgender male, the Department justifying this by overcrowding. The court found that the Department's own standard operating procedures prescribe accommodation appropriate to gender identity where feasible and safe, that no basis existed for refusing single accommodation, and ordered housing in a single cell or with inmates of the same gender identity.

Violence against visibly trans people remains the principal physical risk in the province. On 26 December 2024 Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old transgender woman from Soshanguve living in Winterveld, was assaulted at a tavern in Tshwane at about 1:30 am after a man began saying gay and lesbian people 'don't deserve to live'; he smashed a bottle into her face as she lit a cigarette, saying 'I told you I'm gonna kill you', leaving deep cuts to her mouth, lips, nose, cheek and forehead that were stitched at Kgabo Clinic. She opened an assault case at Dube Police Station, which as of 6 January 2025 had shown no progress.

Nationally, OUT LGBT Well-being's December 2024 rights watch recorded five LGBTQIA+ murders in that month alone, and lesbians and trans people have been murdered, beaten and subjected to 'corrective rape', including among pupils, with activists accusing police of negligent handling of cases and ActionAid condemning impunity. Mismatched documents remain a daily hazard: an analysis published in January 2026 by Mikhail Petersen of Gender Dynamix describes trans people facing humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for 'fraud' when identity documents do not match presentation, and Gender Dynamix's 2024 report records a trans woman turned away from filing a domestic-violence case after showing her ID, with police mocking her. Facilities access is contested rather than settled: a 2024 analysis in PER/PELJ concludes that trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in facility access, so venue rules are expected to vary rather than rest on a single national rule. Gender-affirming care is lawful and available, from age 16 for hormone therapy and 18 for surgery or younger with parental consent, but private care is concentrated in the major cities and public systems face long waits. Partner and family recognition is broad, the Civil Union Act having been in force since 2006, with court decisions extending to same-sex couples covering immigration, employment and pension benefits and joint adoption.
tangentialFactors:
The evidentiary base for hate-crime levels in Gauteng is thin. The first representative quantitative provincial study was 'Hate Crimes Against Gay and Lesbian People in Gauteng: Prevalence, Consequences and Contributing Factors', a Joint Working Group initiative conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being with the UNISA Centre for Applied Psychology (Wells and Polders) in 2003/04, with a partner roster including Behind the Mask, Triangle Project, GALA and the Durban Lesbian & Gay Community & Health Centre.

The companion national review accompanying the Love Not Hate campaign research (GALA-hosted, conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being, 2016) states that only three quantitative studies of LGBT hate crime have ever been done in South Africa: the 2003 study across Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal and Western Cape, a 2010 North West province study, and the 2016 national campaign study. No province-wide quantitative update to the 2003/04 Gauteng findings appears in the inventory.

Human Rights Watch and other legal commentators warned before the May 2024 enactment that the hate-speech provisions are vague and burden free expression, though the statute converts protection into a defined offence framework rather than only a sentencing consideration.

Protection machinery exists at national level: a Department of Justice National Task Team from 2011, a National Intervention Strategy for LGBTI Communities from April 2014 with a rapid response team for unsolved cases, a Justice Ministry programme against gender-based and LGBTI violence launched in the 2010s, and the 2024 Hate Crimes Act. Enforcement records remain uneven against that machinery.

Discrimination and harassment complaints, including hate speech, are heard by the Equality Court under PEPUDA, and the 2024 Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act adds a statutory offence framework where hate speech requires a clear intention to be harmful, incite harm or promote hatred. outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Department of Correctional Services standard operating procedures are implemented in practice across Gauteng facilities remains unresolved; Lawyers for Human Rights litigated a transgender prisoner's conditions of detention earlier in 2025 and rights organisations questioned implementation, while the Mokoena judgment converts the obligations into binding equality-court remedies for that case.

No post-2016 province-level quantitative measurement of hate-crime prevalence against LGBT people in Gauteng is present in the inventory, so the 2003/04 study remains the most recent representative provincial dataset on record.

The inventory does not resolve the outcome of the assault case Aobakwe Mahlobo opened at Dube Police Station; the latest sourced reporting, of 6 January 2025, records no progress.

Facility access for trans and non-binary people in Gauteng is not governed by a settled rule in the sources; the 2024 PER/PELJ analysis argues trans people do not in practice experience equal protection, and venue-level practice is not surveyed.

Whether the October 2021 gender-neutral identification plan has reached legislation is unresolved in the inventory, which records only that officials expected the change to take a few years.
